BREAKING: The White House publishes the details of the US-Venezuela oil deal and announces that Venezuela has granted North American Blue Energy Partners 100-year concessions for 17 oil fields. 

Details include:

1. The 17 fields contain ~65 billion barrels of proven oil reserves

2. The US government receives a 35% equity stake in NABEP's parent company at "zero cost to taxpayers"

3. The US receives the right to purchase 20% of all current and future production at production cost

4. The US also receives the right of first refusal to purchase the remaining 80% of production

5. The US government receives veto power over board appointments, while a majority of NABEP's board must be US citizens

6. NABEP plans to invest up to $100 billion into Venezuelan oil infrastructure to rapidly increase production

7. Venezuela is expected to receive ~$200 billion in royalty and tax payments over the first 25 years

The White House is calling this the "biggest oil deal in world history."

BREAKING: US Total Factor Productivity (TFP) rose +1.10% in the 12 months ending Q2 2026, the lowest growth rate since Q2 2025.

TFP is a key measure of underlying economic productivity, capturing how efficiently labor and capital are used to produce goods and services.

This follows +1.61% growth over the 12 months ending Q1 2026.

Since ChatGPT's release, total factor productivity has increased +2.45%.

By comparison, TFP over the same period following Netscape Navigator's 1994 release, one of the first widely adopted web browsers, grew +7.50%, more than 3x the current AI-era pace.

Meanwhile, utilization-adjusted TFP, which removes the impact of changes in how intensively workers and machines are used, fell -0.42% in the 12 months ending Q2 2026, its weakest reading since Q1 2023.

This may be a better measure of productivity because it shows whether output is rising from genuine efficiency gains, rather than simply from workers and machines being utilized more.

The AI Revolution has yet to translate into a meaningful productivity boom.

We are still early.

US stocks have never been this disconnected from each other:

The median 63-day correlation between individual S&P 500 stocks and the index itself is down to +0.10, the lowest on record.

This measures how closely individual stocks move with the broader index, with a reading this low meaning the index is being driven by a small group of stocks while most move independently.

This figure has dropped -71% over the last 5 months.

By comparison, during the March 2025 selloff, the median 63-day correlation surged to as much as +0.76.

To put this into perspective, the previous all-time low was +0.16 following the 2000 Dot-Com Bubble burst.

The market is more concentrated than ever.

Gavin Baker says the future for the world's biggest companies is open models and private context:

"I think the future is an ensemble of models. There's a Pareto curve. No one model is going to be the best at everything."

"For the global 1,000 biggest companies, you're going to take whatever the best open-source model is. I think probably in the very near future, that's going to be an Nvidia model."

"Everybody says 'Well, in a world where open-source wins, who funds the training?' Chip companies can fund the training."

"It's trivial to do a $50 to $100 billion training run for Jensen, but I do think you're going to see American open-source led by Nvidia get really close to the frontier."

"Sharing your own enterprise context, that's truly your IP, that's truly the value of your company, the context embedded in all of your data, sharing that with a frontier lab may be hazardous for your financial health."

"I think what you'll see these companies do is they'll have their own model on their data, and it will work with one or two other frontier models, checking each other... I think that feels like a very likely future to me."

@GavinSBaker @DavidGeorge83

tweets.text:
⚡️ The market is still heavily focused on models, Nvidia and token prices but who is going to power, finance, insure and ultimately monetize the gigantic physical infrastructure being built behind AI? - FT

🇺🇸 In the US, the number of data centers above 100MW could almost triple if all announced projects are completed. However, it is important to keep in mind that a large part of the pipeline is still only planned and not actually under construction. The bottleneck is increasingly electricity, grid connections, transformers, turbines, permits and land. Some campuses now involve several gigawatts of planned capacity.

💰 This is structurally very bullish for the entire power chain (grids, utilities, gas turbines, batteries, cooling systems, electrical equipment and potentially nuclear) but it also makes the whole build-out much riskier because the amounts that need to be financed are becoming enormous. Meta and BlackRock’s 14bn dollars El Paso campus is a good example because hyperscalers are increasingly relying on JVs, dedicated vehicles, private debt, long-term contracts and various guarantees to fund their Capex. Not necessarily unhealthy but as you know this means that the AI boom is becoming increasingly dependent on credit markets and on these assets generating adequate returns for 15 or 20 years.

⚠️ The unit cost of intelligence is falling rapidly while the physical cost of building the infrastructure required to produce it is exploding. As long as lower prices trigger an even larger increase in usage, everything works but the problem would emerge if algorithmic and hardware efficiency gains started to outpace demand growth. In that case, we could eventually end up with far more capacity than is actually needed.

🤔 For the moment, I would pay less attention to the hundreds of data centers being announced and much more attention to three things. 

➡ How many actually move into construction? 
➡ How many successfully secure power? 
➡ At what cost of capital they are financed?

This is where we will ultimately distinguish a genuine industrial supercycle from the future stranded assets of the AI boom.

*FT link: https://t.co/SeyJxgyVeo

🇰🇷 The AI and semiconductor cycle has become powerful enough to distort an entire country’s macro data on its own.

📊 In August, Korean exports jumped 72.5% year-on-year on a working-day adjusted basis, with chip exports up 209% and computer shipments up 419% ⚠. Moreover, semiconductors now account for almost half of the country’s exports and explain the vast majority of the recent increase.

➡️ HBM, DRAM, NAND, servers and computing equipment are all benefiting from the explosion in AI and data-center spending. However, these numbers should not be interpreted as evidence of a broad-based global recovery as several traditional Korean industries remain far less dynamic. Even the 119% surge in exports to China reflects Asian electronics supply chains to a large extent rather than a genuine rebound in Chinese domestic demand. South Korea is especially becoming a thermometer for global AI capex.

🏦 For the Bank of Korea, these numbers clearly reinforce its hawkish shift. It has now delivered two consecutive rate hikes, raised its 2026 growth forecast to 3.3%, and still faces relatively sticky core inflation. With growth this strong, there is almost no reason to rush into rate cuts. This also supports the won as a huge trade surplus, tighter monetary policy and a stronger currency help reduce imported inflation.

As long as hyperscalers and the rest of the ecosystem keep spending aggressively, this is extremely supportive, but the greater this concentration becomes, the more a slowdown in capex, easing memory shortages or a reversal in pricing could have an outsized macro impact.

*Bloomberg link: https://t.co/kJFE8usiJx

tweets.text:
The Fed no longer controls the long end. For 30 years the 10-year yield moved almost only in the 3-day window around Fed meetings. Since 2022 it has climbed ~4 points, and almost none of that came on Fed days.

Treasury supply and a rising term premium did the work, not the dot plot. With Warsh dropping forward guidance, the long end now trades on issuance and data.

So if you are waiting for Fed cuts to drag down mortgage rates or the 10-year at 4.75%, you are watching the wrong lever. The market prices $40T of supply now, and it wants to be paid more to hold it. $TLT stays heavy.

tweets.text:
Macro investors make the most money by betting against major trends when they become unsustainable.

If you ask me which major macro trend looks the most unsustainable today, I would not point to rising US long-end yields or the BOJ continuing to stay behind the curve.

I would point instead to the chart below: Chinese real investment growth has collapsed to a staggering -7%—a historical low outside of the initial COVID-19 shock.

In my view, this is arguably the most unsustainable macro trend in the world today—and one that investors should pay very close attention to, and potentially position for a reversal, in the coming quarters.
